w: Camp Nou has been FC Barcelona's home since 1957 and is mid-renovation toward a planned 105,000 seats, the largest capacity in Europe. It hosted European Cup/Champions League finals in 1989 and 1999, the 1992 Olympic football final, and the opening match of the 1982 World Cup.
s: Barcelona's home since 1957, rebuilding to 105,000 seats

w: Stadio Olimpico opened in 1953 with Italy vs Hungary and seats over 70,000, the largest sports venue in Rome. Built from 1928 in the Foro Italico complex, it has been shared by Lazio and Roma since opening. Ciro Immobile holds the stadium scoring record with 120 goals.
s: Rome's biggest stadium, shared by Lazio and Roma since 1953
_facts: Home of Lazio and Roma since 1953
Ciro Immobile: 120 goals, most at the stadium

w: Stade Velodrome has been Olympique de Marseille's home since it opened in 1937 and holds 67,394, the second-largest stadium in France after Stade de France. It staged matches at the 1938 and 1998 World Cups, three European Championships, two Rugby World Cups, and 2024 Olympic football.
s: Marseille's Ligue 1 home, hosted three World Cups' games
_facts: Home of Olympique de Marseille since 1937

w: Selhurst Park opened in 1924, designed by Archibald Leitch, and has been Crystal Palace's home ground since. It hosted football at the 1948 London Olympics and was shared by Charlton Athletic from 1985-91 and Wimbledon from 1991-2003, in the London Borough of Croydon.
s: Crystal Palace's Leitch-designed ground since 1924

w: Celtic Park, nicknamed Paradise, has been Celtic's home since the club moved to the site in 1892; it holds 60,411, the largest football stadium in Scotland. A record crowd of 83,500 watched an Old Firm derby here on 1 January 1938. Terraces were rebuilt into an all-seated stadium by 1998.
s: Celtic's Parkhead fortress, Scotland's biggest ground

w: Stadion Maksimir, built in 1912, is Dinamo Zagreb's home ground and has hosted Croatia's national team since 1990. Current seating capacity is 25,912, expandable to 35,423. Renovated in 1948, 1998 and 2011, its east stand has stayed closed since a 2020 earthquake damaged it.
s: Dinamo Zagreb's 1912-built home in Maksimir

w: Craven Cottage has been Fulham FC's home since 1896, on the Thames beside Bishop's Park on the site of a former royal hunting lodge. Capacity is 27,782; the record attendance, 49,335, was set against Millwall in 1938. It was formerly also home to rugby league side Fulham RLFC.
s: Fulham's riverside ground since 1896, ex-hunting lodge

w: San Mames Stadium opened on 16 September 2013, replacing the old San Mames as Athletic Bilbao's home. Seating 53,331, it is the seventh-largest stadium in Spain and the largest in the Basque Country, standing on Rafael Moreno Pitxitxi Kalea in Bilbao.
s: Athletic Bilbao's 2013 replacement for old San Mames

w: Ibrox Stadium, designed by Archibald Leitch and opened as Ibrox Park in 1899, is Rangers' home and Scotland's third-largest football ground at 51,700 all-seated. A record British crowd of 118,567 saw Rangers face Celtic there in January 1939. It was largely rebuilt after a 1971 disaster.
s: Rangers' Leitch-designed Ibrox, rebuilt after 1971

w: Stadion Poljud opened in September 1979 as Hajduk Split's home ground in the Poljud district. Original capacity of 55,000 was raised to 62,000 in the 1980s before seating cut it to 33,987. It hosted the 1990 European Athletics Championships and the Ultra Europe festival from 2013-19.
s: Hajduk Split's home since 1979, hosted Ultra Europe

w: Estadio Benito Villamarin has been Real Betis's home stadium in Sevilla, Spain, since its completion in 1929. The ground has served the club continuously since then and today holds 60,721 spectators, making it one of Spain's larger football stadiums nearly a century after it first opened.
s: Real Betis's Sevilla ground since 1929

w: Jan Breydel Stadium, built in 1975, is the shared home of rival clubs Club Brugge and Cercle Brugge in Sint-Andries, Bruges. It holds 29,042 seats and was known as Olympiastadion with 18,000 seats before Euro 2000. Named after Jan Breydel, an instigator of the 1302 Bruges Matins uprising.
s: Shared home of Club Brugge and Cercle Brugge since 1975
_facts: Shared home of Club Brugge and Cercle Brugge
Named after Jan Breydel of the 1302 Bruges Matins

w: Windsor Park is Linfield's home ground in Belfast, on land the club owns while the Irish Football Association operates the stadium and pays Linfield rent on behalf of the Northern Ireland national football team. It usually hosts the Irish Cup final and is officially the National Football Stadium.
s: Linfield-owned, Northern Ireland's national stadium
_facts: Owned by Linfield, operated by the Irish FA
Usually hosts the Irish Cup final

w: Accor Arena, originally the Palais Omnisports de Paris-Bercy, is an indoor arena and concert hall in the Bercy district of Paris's 12th arrondissement. Its pyramidal shape has sloping walls covered with grass. It seats 7,000 to 20,300 and has hosted an annual martial arts festival since 1985.
s: Paris arena with grass-covered pyramid walls
_facts: Indoor arena and concert hall in Paris
Hosts annual martial arts festival since 1985

w: Fortuna Arena, in Prague-Vrsovice, is the biggest and most modern football stadium in the Czech Republic at 19,370 capacity. It is Slavia Prague's home venue and occasionally hosts the national team; Bohemians 1905 and Viktoria Plzen also played home matches there. It staged the 2013 UEFA Super Cup.
s: Czech Republic's biggest, most modern football ground
_facts: Biggest, most modern stadium in Czech Republic

w: San Marino Stadium, formerly Stadio Olimpico di Serravalle, first opened in 1969 in Serravalle, San Marino, and is used mainly for football. It serves as the national stadium of San Marino, hosting the country's football matches in the small city-state bordering Italy near Rimini.
s: San Marino's national stadium since 1969

w: Stozice Stadium, designed by Sadar + Vuga architects, is Slovenia's biggest football stadium, located in the Bezigrad district of Ljubljana. It is home to Olimpija Ljubljana and the main venue of the Slovenia national football team, forming part of the wider Stozice Sports Park complex.
s: Slovenia's biggest football stadium, home of Olimpija

w: Millerntor-Stadion, built in 1961 with an original 32,000 capacity, is FC St. Pauli's home ground on the Heiligengeistfeld near Hamburg's Reeperbahn. American football side the Blue Devils also play there, and Prince performed a concert at the stadium in 1988.
s: St. Pauli's Reeperbahn-adjacent Millerntor ground
_facts: Also used by Blue Devils American football team
Prince performed a concert there in 1988

w: The Valley has been Charlton Athletic's home ground since 1919, apart from spells of exile in 1923-24 and 1985-92, and holds 27,111 in Charlton, southeast London. Charlton Athletic Women have played home matches there since 2024. Charlton railway station sits a three-minute walk away.
s: Charlton Athletic's home since 1919, near the Thames
_facts: Charlton Athletic Women play there since 2024

w: Copper Box Arena was built for the 2012 Summer Olympics in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, London, and was originally known as the Handball Arena. Beyond handball it staged modern pentathlon events - fencing, shooting, swimming, show jumping and running - and served as the goalball venue for the 2012 Paralympics.
s: 2012 Olympics handball arena in Queen Elizabeth Park
_facts: Located in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park

w: Fratton Park, constructed in 1899, has been Portsmouth FC's only home ground, making it the sole professional English football ground on Portsea Island rather than the British mainland. It staged England's first Football League match under floodlights in 1956; capacity is now 20,867, all-seated since 1996.
s: Portsmouth's only home since 1899, on Portsea Island
_facts: Only English pro football ground off the mainland
First English League match under floodlights, 1956

w: Tynecastle Park, nicknamed Tynie, has been Heart of Midlothian's home ground on the present Gorgie site since 1886. A UEFA category four stadium seating 19,852, it is Scotland's sixth-largest football ground and has hosted Scotland internationals plus Scottish Cup and League Cup semi-finals.
s: Hearts' Gorgie ground, Scotland's 6th biggest
_facts: Home of Heart of Midlothian since 1886

w: Valeriy Lobanovskyi Dynamo Stadium, built in 1934 as Vsevolod Balitsky Dynamo Stadium for the Ukrainian SSR Dynamo sports society, is Dynamo Kyiv's secondary home ground alongside the larger NSC Olympiyskiy. It seats 16,873 and also hosts Ukraine national team exhibition matches, near the former NKVD building in Kyiv.
s: Dynamo Kyiv's 1934-built secondary Kyiv home
_facts: Built in 1934 for the Dynamo sports society
Also hosts Ukraine national team exhibition games

w: Daugava National Stadium first opened in Riga, Latvia, in 1927 and hosts football and athletics alongside adjacent arenas in its sports complex. Designated a facility of national importance since 1992, it is owned by the Latvian government and now also carries the sponsored name BTA Daugava Stadium.
s: Riga's 1927 national stadium for football, athletics
_facts: National stadium of Latvia, in Riga

w: Stadion Balgarska Armia was CSKA Sofia's home ground in Sofia's Borisova Gradina park, holding 22,995 seats across four sectors before closure in late 2023. Demolished in 2024, it is being rebuilt as an 18,540-seat football-only venue, with CSKA playing meanwhile at Vasil Levski National Stadium.
s: CSKA Sofia's demolished 2024 ground, being rebuilt

w: Basaksehir Fatih Terim Stadium opened officially on 26 July 2014 in Istanbul's Basaksehir district, named for Turkish footballer and manager Fatih Terim. Home to Super Lig club Istanbul Basaksehir FK, it holds 17,156 and cost about 178 million lira; Qarabag FK used it for 2020-21 Europa League matches instead of Baku.
s: Istanbul Basaksehir's 2014 stadium named for Fatih Terim

w: Tallaght Stadium is an association football ground in Tallaght, South Dublin, first announced by Shamrock Rovers in July 1996. It is now owned and operated by South Dublin County Council, with Shamrock Rovers serving as the anchor tenants of the venue in the south Dublin suburb.
s: Shamrock Rovers' Tallaght home in South Dublin
_facts: Announced by Shamrock Rovers in July 1996
Owned by South Dublin County Council

w: Stadio Pier Luigi Penzo, first opened in 1913, is Venice's largest sports facility and the home ground of Venezia FC. Named after World War I pilot Pier Luigi Penzo, it is Italy's second-oldest continually used stadium, after Genoa's Stadio Luigi Ferraris.
s: Venezia FC's ground, Italy's 2nd-oldest in use
_facts: Italy's second-oldest stadium in continual use

w: Ali Sami Yen Stadium was Galatasaray's home ground in Istanbul's Sisli district from 1964 to 2010, named after the club's founder. The all-seater venue held 23,477 spectators in the Mecidiyekoy quarter, at the center of the European side of the city, before Galatasaray moved to a new stadium.
s: Galatasaray's Istanbul home from 1964 to 2010
_facts: Named after club founder Ali Sami Yen

w: Stadionul Steaua, informally Ghencea Stadium, was FC Steaua Bucuresti's home ground in Bucharest, inaugurated 9 April 1974 with a 2-2 friendly against OFK Belgrade. Gheorghe Tataru scored the stadium's first goal. It was entirely demolished in 2018 and replaced by a new all-seater stadium opened in 2021.
s: Steaua Bucuresti's demolished 1974 ground, rebuilt 2021
_facts: Replaced by a new stadium opened in 2021

w: Stade Pierre de Coubertin is an indoor arena in Paris and the home venue of the Paris Saint-Germain Handball team. Named for the founder of the modern Olympics, it seats 4,200 spectators for basketball games, hosting a range of indoor sporting events across the French capital.
s: Paris handball arena named for the Olympics' founder
_facts: Named after the modern Olympics' founder

w: The County Ground has been Swindon Town FC's home since 1896, currently holding 14,753 all-seated after a capacity unchanged since the mid-1990s. A record crowd of 32,000 watched an FA Cup third-round tie against Arsenal on 15 January 1972. Swindon Cricket Club's ground, also called The County Ground, sits just north.
s: Swindon Town's home since 1896, near the cricket ground
_facts: Home of Swindon Town FC since 1896
Record crowd 32,000 vs Arsenal, 1972 FA Cup
Swindon Cricket Club's ground sits nearby

w: Stadionul National was a multi-purpose stadium in Bucharest holding 60,120 people, used for major events including anniversaries of the Romanian state, Liberation from Fascist Occupation Day on 23 August, televised propaganda events, and the Cintarea Romaniei cultural festival during the communist era.
s: Communist-era Bucharest stadium for state events
_facts: Hosted Liberation from Fascist Occupation Day

w: Cukaricki Stadium, colloquially Stadion na Banovom Brdu, is FK Cukaricki's home ground in Belgrade, Serbia, seating 4,070 spectators. The multi-purpose venue anchors the Banovo Brdo area of the city and serves as the base for the Serbian top-flight club's home matches.
s: FK Cukaricki's small Belgrade home ground

w: Wladyslaw Krol Municipal Stadium, also known as Stadion Miejski LKS Lodz, is a football stadium in Lodz, Poland, with a capacity of 18,029 seats. It serves as the home ground for LKS Lodz, hosting the club's matches in the city.
s: Lodz football stadium seating 18,029
_facts: Also known as Wladyslaw Krol Municipal Stadium

w: Bozsik Jozsef Stadion was a UEFA category 4 multi-use stadium in Budapest and the home ground of Budapest Honved FC, holding 8,760 spectators. Named after Hungarian footballer Jozsef Bozsik, the old stadium hosted the club's matches for decades before being completely demolished in 2019.
s: Demolished 2019 Budapest Honved home ground

w: Alexander Stadium, in Perry Barr, Birmingham, is the United Kingdom's largest athletics stadium, seating 18,000 across four stands after a 72 million pound redevelopment completed in 2022. It hosted the opening ceremony and athletics events at the 2022 Commonwealth Games and staged the British Grand Prix.
s: UK's biggest athletics stadium, 2022 Games host
_facts: Home of Birchfield Harriers athletics club

w: Taksim Stadium was Istanbul's first football stadium, converted from the 19th-century Taksim Artillery Barracks in 1921 and home to Galatasaray, Fenerbahce and Besiktas. Holding about 8,000 spectators, it closed in 1939 and was demolished in 1940 to make way for Taksim Gezi Parki.
s: Istanbul's first ground, demolished for Gezi Park
_facts: Home to Galatasaray, Fenerbahce and Besiktas

w: Theodoros Vardinogiannis Stadium, nicknamed Yedi Kule, was built in 1951 as OFI's home ground in Heraklion, Crete. Its nickname references the Heptapyrgion fortress, an Ottoman-era stronghold, evoking the stadium's fortress-like ambiance and symbolizing strength and resilience for the club.
s: Heraklion's Yedi Kule, OFI's fortress-named ground
_facts: Home of OFI, in Heraklion, Crete
Nicknamed Yedi Kule after Heptapyrgion fortress
